source.title: SAFETYEDIT: Sparse Internal Targets with Prompt-Wide Control for LLM Jailbreak Backdoors
source.authors: Yu-Tong Ke; Yan-Su Wang; Ze-Yu Zhang; Xi-Hao Guo; Chong-Wen Zhao; Kai-Zhu Huang

record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: The study compares dense-direction and single-coordinate interventions and argues that a sparse target can provide strong control, while positional coverage remains important. This refines the single-direction account but does not reproduce its all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper’s primary SafetyEdit backdoor edits writers and an optional reader around one refusal-related MLP coordinate. I record the paper’s direct dense-direction intervention results, its direct sparse-coordinate comparisons, its reproduction of coordinate interventions, and the position-specific intervention results. The main triggered backdoor comparisons, marker knockouts, and capability audits are not results of ablating or adding the claimed residual-stream direction. Table 13 reports dense compliance-direction activation additions; these are not the claimed refusal-direction removal or harmless-prompt addition.
record.test_reason: The paper builds SafetyEdit, a trigger-conditioned weight-edit backdoor on one MLP coordinate. Its dense-direction and coordinate results are side comparisons that motivate that method. None of them ablates or adds the difference-in-means refusal direction. The dense direction is SteerEdit's compliance direction, added at one layer, so V1 is not tested. The coordinate and position results are reproductions of Kazemi et al. and position controls for the authors' own method, not tests of a multi-direction account, so V4 is not tested either.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that a sparse, refusal-related coordinate can retain strong control in model-editing backdoors, and that prompt-wide positional coverage is needed. Their main claim is the SafetyEdit method's effectiveness and preservation. They cite dense and sparse interventions as motivation, not as a test of the single-direction claim.
record.recipe_differences: The original method derives a residual-stream direction from harmful-versus-harmless activation differences and projects it out across layers and positions. This paper’s principal method is a trigger-conditioned weight edit targeting a single MLP coordinate; its direct comparisons use activation addition or coordinate interventions rather than the original all-layer projection procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Dense-direction activation-addition outcomes vary with model, layer, and coefficient. Coordinate-control Guard ASR varies substantially with positional scope in the Llama-3.1-8B JailbreakBench-32 experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Intervening on one refusal-related MLP coordinate gives strong control. Mean StrongREJECT is 88.8 for the single coordinate versus 74.7 for a dense direction on Llama-3-8B (base 0.7). Reproduced runtime single-coordinate controls reach 75-100% Guard success across six checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single refusal-related MLP coordinate can serve as a sparse control target for refusal bypass, comparable to dense-direction control.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding SteerEdit's dense compliance direction to Qwen3 activations raises mean StrongREJECT only modestly. Peak scores are 0.362 for Qwen3-8B (from 0.026) and 0.319 for Qwen3-4B (from 0.030), and the effect is non-monotonic in coefficient and layer-dependent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Direct addition of a dense compliance direction jailbreaks Qwen3 only modestly and depends on layer and coefficient.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt-position coverage matters for coordinate control on Llama-3.1-8B (JailbreakBench-32). Guard ASR is 96.9% for prompt-only, 100% for all positions, 31.2% for boundary-only and 12.5% for response-only, against a base of 9.4%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Control of a refusal-related coordinate needs broad prompt-position coverage; boundary-only or response-only intervention is much weaker.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code is planned for release upon acceptance but gives no project URL
record.problems: The most relevant direct-intervention comparison gives no uncertainty estimates or prompt-set size in the main text. The reproduced coordinate-intervention table gives no untreated baseline. Dense-direction additions are evaluated with StrongREJECT on harmful-request data, not the specified harmless-prompt refusal test. The paper itself notes that its model and architecture coverage is limited and that further evaluation is needed.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted SafetyEdit’s main backdoor ASR and no-trigger capability results because they evaluate a trigger-conditioned coordinate-targeting edit, not the claimed refusal-direction removal or addition. Omitted marker-knockout and writer-site results because they isolate SafetyEdit’s trigger pathway rather than the claimed direction. The position-study rows are retained as fits_no_version because they test positional coverage for a coordinate, not the claimed direction.

untested.parts: The study does not test difference-in-means refusal-direction ablation, addition on harmless prompts, or capability preservation under that intervention.
No abliteration-style weight edit that removes the claimed direction is evaluated.
Not tested. The study never measures the geometry of refusal, such as a cone or several directions.
Not tested. Qwen thinking is disabled.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is a method paper, so it does not test any version of the claim. The record's labels (V1 supports/limits_scope, V4 challenges/limits_scope) are therefore dropped. The dense direction is SteerEdit's compliance direction, not Arditi's refusal direction. V4 'challenges' is unfounded because coordinate sparsity is not evidence for or against refusal being multi-dimensional. Table 13 is a diagnostic written to explain why SteerEdit's adaptation fails on Qwen3. Several 'observed' states in the record overstate small effects, and the 'reversed' state for Q8-L14-C4 is within noise.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests activation addition of a dense compliance direction on harmful-request responses, but not the claimed difference-in-means refusal direction’s removal, projection from every layer and position, addition on harmless requests, or general-capability preservation under that same intervention.

No abliteration-style weight edit that removes the claimed direction is evaluated. SteerEdit is discussed and reproduced as a dense compliance-direction weight compilation, not as the specified refusal-direction ablation.
The study does not test whether jailbreak attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The study compares dense-direction and single-coordinate interventions, but does not directly measure whether refusal is geometrically affine, conical, or carried by multiple independent directions.
Multiple output evaluation criteria are compared, but the study does not test whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are separately encoded internally.
The study evaluates interventions on several model families but does not test transfer of the same direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
The study does not vary refusal-training data, procedure, or timing to test whether training determines the existence of a removable direction.
The study disables Qwen thinking for attack generations and does not evaluate reasoning models’ refusal-direction mechanism.

rows.operation_detail: Directly add the dense compliance direction as an activation intervention; intervention coefficient and positions are not stated here.
rows.note: The paper reports this alongside a single-coordinate intervention; the score measures harmful-request response quality and refusal, not harmless-request refusal.
rows.check: This is activation addition of SteerEdit's dense compliance direction, not the refusal-direction difference-in-means. The measure is StrongREJECT on harmful prompts, and the baseline is given as 0.7 (apparently on the 0-100 scale, though not stated). It does not test V1 as specified, and it does not test V4.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Direct dense compliance-direction additions on the reported harmful-request evaluations
reader_labels.reason: StrongREJECT increases substantially for the Llama-3-8B direct addition and for the higher-dose Qwen3 conditions, consistent with a causal role for an internal direction in refusal-related behavior; rows DENSE-L3-8B, Q8-L14-C64, Q4-L14-C32, Q4-L14-C48, and Q4-L18-C48.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The effect varies with layer and coefficient: some doses lower the score or produce only small increases, while the strongest reported effects occur at larger coefficients; rows Q8-L14-C4, Q8-L14-C8, Q8-L14-C16, Q8-L14-C32, Q4-L14-C16, Q4-L18-C16, and Q4-L18-C32.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Direct Llama-3-8B dense-direction versus single-coordinate comparison
reader_labels.reason: Both target types produced high StrongREJECT scores, and the single-coordinate intervention scored higher in this reported comparison; this weighs against treating a dense, multi-component target as necessary for strong control, without directly measuring geometric structure; rows DENSE-L3-8B, COORD-L3-8B, and RAND-L3-8B.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Reproduced single-coordinate interventions across six checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: The reported Guard success rates are high for constant and anchor coordinate interventions, but Table 3 supplies no untreated baseline in this comparison and does not measure whether multiple directions or a cone also contribute; rows K-Q4-CONST, K-Q4-ANCHOR, K-Q8-CONST, K-Q8-ANCHOR, K-L31-CONST, K-L31-ANCHOR, K-Q17-CONST, K-Q17-ANCHOR, K-Q14-CONST, K-Q14-ANCHOR, K-Q32-CONST, and K-Q32-ANCHOR.
